patch.value: Point-in-time reconstruction gate: prove every item at every recorded version replays exactly from its history stream alone

The restorability promise is that any item can be returned to any version at any time, and point-in-time reads already exist. What is not proven is the general case: that for every item in a workspace, and every version in its stream, replaying the stream from the beginning reproduces exactly the state that read returns, using nothing but the immutable history. Today's coverage tests the mechanism on chosen cases; the promise is universal and therefore needs a universal check. Make it a gate: for a workspace corpus that includes real-shaped history — items that were renamed, retyped, reparented, redacted, compacted, restored, merged from divergent branches, and closed and reopened — replay every version of every item from its stream and assert byte-identical agreement with the point-in-time projection, with the item file itself used only as an independent third comparison and never as the source. Disagreement is a data-integrity defect by definition. Compaction and redaction are the interesting cases and must be covered explicitly, since both rewrite what a replay can see and must preserve reconstructability of every version they claim to retain.

For every item and every recorded version in the test corpus, replay from the history stream alone reproduces the point-in-time projection exactly; The current item file is used only as an independent third comparison, never as an input to the replay, asserted by the test's construction; The corpus includes items that were renamed, retyped, reparented, redacted, compacted, restored, merged from divergent branches, and closed and reopened; Compacted streams are covered explicitly: every version the compaction claims to retain still replays exactly, and versions it dropped are reported as intentionally unavailable rather than silently wrong; Redacted streams replay to a state that omits the redacted content while keeping every other field and the chain verifiable; A mismatch fails the gate with the item, version, and diverging field named, so the failure is diagnosable without rerunning by hand
The restorability promise is a checked property of every item and every version, not a demonstrated capability of the restore command
Restorability and provable history are the durability promise; a promise that holds for the cases someone remembered to test is not a promise
Adds an exhaustive replay check over a history corpus; expected to surface reconstruction gaps around compaction, redaction, and merge-union streams
Any recorded state of any item is provably reachable from immutable history alone

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Round-trip fidelity probed on the shipped 2026.7.25 build, so this gate's corpus can be built around cases that already hold and the one that does not. Isolated sandbox, one item taken through create, update, dependency add, note_add, files_add, comment_add, update.

Backward-then-forward restore is exact. pm restore <id> 1 reduced the item to its creation state and dropped notes, files, comments, and the dependency row to zero — correct point-in-time semantics, not loss. pm restore <id> 6 then returned every one of them: title, description, the related dependency row, 1 note, 1 comment, 1 file link. Nothing in the annotation or link families needed a separate recovery path.

Delete is a tombstone and is fully reversible. After pm delete <id> --message "...": the item file is gone, the history stream is retained, pm get reports not found, pm get <id> --at 1 still returns the full point-in-time item, and pm restore <id> 1 resurrects it with 10 fields restored and it reappears in pm list. The delete op is recorded in the stream (ops: create, comment_add, restore, delete). The read-surface half — that pm get discloses none of this — is filed separately as pm-nb4zwz.

The corpus gap this leaves is version identity. History entries carry no version field; the record keys are ts, author, author_source, agent_harness, op, patch, before_hash, after_hash, message. Version addressing for restore and --at is therefore ordinal position in the stream, while the stable identity available is after_hash. That is fine in a single lane, and I verified pm get --at 2 is stable across a branch merge, but it means this gate's compaction and merge clauses are asserting something about ordinals rather than about content-addressed states. Worth deciding explicitly in the corpus design whether a retained version's identity is its ordinal or its after_hash, because pruning and reanchoring act on the two differently.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Reconstruction verified end to end on 2026-07-26 against a doubly-mutated item, which is a stronger test than a single-write fixture because it proves the replay composes.

pm-j1fj is a closed item from the v2026.6.30 window. Today it received two independent mutations from two different lanes: a release attribution stamp and a set of evidence-derived relationship edges. Reading it at a timestamp before those writes returns release absent, updated_at 2026-06-30T05:34:40.038Z, and 2 dependencies. Reading it now returns release v2026.6.30, updated_at 2026-07-26T17:17:07.733Z, and 5 dependencies. The historical projection is not a stale cache — it is reconstructed from the stream, and it correctly excludes both of today's writes while preserving the pre-existing edges.

What this does and does not prove, for the record this item keeps: it demonstrates single-item point-in-time projection over a multi-write day, which is the pm-hib1 capability that already shipped. It does not demonstrate workspace-level projection (pm-5gf0xf) and it does not constitute the reconstruction gate this item owns, because nothing asserts it in CI. It is a positive control worth pinning as a fixture: an item with a create-era baseline, a long quiet period, and two same-day writes from different lanes is exactly the shape a naive implementation gets wrong.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: Reconstruction spot-check on a freshly authored stream, 2026-07-28: pm-jkbqt8 with 7 entries replays correctly at every probed version — --at 1 returns the create state with 0 dependencies and the estimate already set, --at 3 returns 10 dependencies after the wiring mutation, --at 7 matches head, and all three report reconstructed true. pm history --verify reports ok true over 7 entries with current_matches_latest true and an empty error list. One reading caveat for whoever builds this gate: the reconstructed projection reports no comments at any version, which is NOT a replay gap — pm get --json omits the comments collection entirely, exactly as it omits notes, so the same item reports 0 through get and 2 through pm comments. A gate that asserts collection equality by diffing pm get output will therefore pass vacuously on comments and notes; it has to read them through their own commands.
